newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian financier turns himself in for jail term.
newsitem.headline: Italian financier turns himself in for jail term.

text.p: Italian financier Sergio Cusani, who helped expose rampant corruption at the heart of Italy's political old guard, turned himself into prison authorities on Wednesday to begin a four year sentence for bribery.
Cusani, the first major personality to be convicted in Italy's "Tangentopoli" (Bribesville) scandals, arrived at Milan's notorious San Vittore prison with suitcase in hand.

"I am at peace with myself. I will try to build something useful for people inside prison, where life carries on even if it's not a very good life," Cusani told reporters before entering the imposing jail.

Cusani was convicted two years ago for his part in a scandal over bribes paid by insurance firm SAI to win contracts from energy group ENI. He was the central figure in another major corruption trial centred on ENI which is currently under appeal.
Italy's highest court confirmed Cusani's jail term on Tuesday and also upheld sentences on former Italian prime minister Bettino Craxi and nine others.

Craxi is in self-imposed exile in Tunisia and is unlikely to return home to face the music. He faces a jail term of five and half years for the SAI saga and has more than 25 years of prison sentences accumulated against him from other trials.
The former premier has said he will not fly back to Italy just to go to jail.

The high court also confirmed sentences against former SAI president Salvatore Ligresti and managing director Fausto Rapisardo, former Christian Democrat party treasurer Severino Citaristi and two former ENI executives.
But Italian media said they would probably not have to go to jail since they had received sentences of less than three years and could qualify for public service.
The Tangentopoli scandals broke in February 1992 when the manager of a Milan old people's home confessed to taking bribes on behalf of Craxi's Socialist party.
His confession led to other confessions and soon prosecutors had cracked open an entrenched system of bribes-for-public contracts involving politicians and businessmen.
Few were spared in the judicial assault. Before Cusani only one other person, an obscure Milan councillor, has actually served a prison term arising from the scandals.
San Vittore prison became a symbol of the scandals in 1993 after former ENI chairman Gabriele Cagliari killed himself in a cell there while under investigation for graft.
Cagliari was one of a number of people to commit suicide in the wake of the scandals.
